PLANT GUIDE · OAKLAND HOLLY

Oakland Holly

Ilex × ‘Magland’ — the holly whose leaves are shaped like an oak’s

A holly in oak’s clothing: a dense evergreen pyramid of glossy, oak-lobed leaves, each edged with 3 to 5 pairs of spines, flushing copper-red as it opens in spring. Its small cream flowers are perfect — both sexes in a single flower — so one plant alone loads itself with orange-red berries that feed songbirds through the winter. No pollinator partner required, no shearing required: the pyramid builds itself.

🔍 Anatomy — Telling It from the Other Hollies

OAKLAND
deep oak lobes, 3–5 pairs of spines, leaves held close — yours
AMERICAN HOLLY
the classic Christmas leaf — spines around a plain oval
OAKLEAF (the parent)
the same oak idea, looser and larger — Oakland is its tighter sport

The identification rests on one look — the leaf is an oak leaf. Each glossy, leathery blade, about 2¾ inches long by 1⅛ wide, is cut into deep lobes carrying 3 to 5 pairs of prominent spines, a silhouette no other common holly wears. American holly (Ilex opaca) keeps the classic Christmas-card leaf — spines marched around a plain oval — and the boxleaf hollies are smaller still and spineless. Oakland’s own parent, Oakleaf™ (Ilex × ‘Conaf’), shares the oak shape, but Oakland was selected from it precisely because it grows denser and more compact, its foliage held closer along the stems and its lobes cut deeper. The second test comes in spring: the flowers are perfect, carrying male and female parts in one small cream flower — where nearly every other holly is male or female, never both — and the new growth flushes reddish-copper before it settles to deep green.

🌿 The names: “Oakland” is pure description — the land of the oak-shaped leaf. Ilex itself is the Latin name of the holm oak, whose foliage hollies have echoed all along; this cultivar simply makes the resemblance unmistakable. The plant began as a single branch sport — one branch growing tighter than the rest — found by Jack Magee at Evergreen Nursery in Poplarville, Mississippi, in 1994, and patented as ‘Magland’ (PP14,417).

🎛️ Conditions — Measured

This is a landscape evergreen built for the long term — a dense, upright pyramid of 12 to 20 feet that nurseries plant by the thousand as screens, hedges, and foundation anchors across Zones 6–9. Martinsburg sits in Zone 6b–7a, squarely in its range, with one condition the extension services repeat: shelter from cold northern winter winds, which scorch the broad evergreen leaves. A rock slope, a wall, or a building at its back — exactly the site in your photo — is the classic answer. Give it moist, slightly acidic, well-drained ground and it asks for very little else.

📋 The Care Card

LightFull sun to part shade. At least 4–6 hours of direct sun keeps the pyramid dense to the ground; in deep shade it opens up and thins. In hot southern sites a little afternoon shade prevents leaf scorch — in West Virginia, full sun is welcome.
WaterKeep the soil evenly moist through the first year or two while the roots spread — a deep drink weekly in dry spells. Once established it is drought-tolerant, though a long dry autumn still deserves a soaking before the ground freezes. It will not tolerate standing water.
SoilMoist, slightly acidic, well-drained is the ideal — pH 5.2–6.8. It adapts to sand, loam, and clay provided drainage is real. In sweet or alkaline soil the leaves yellow between green veins (chlorosis) — the plant’s way of asking for acid.
FeedingOne spring application of a holly/acid-lover fertilizer is plenty for a landscape plant; mulch with 2–3 inches of leaf litter, bark, or pine straw, kept off the trunk. Your plant is already wearing its leaf-litter mulch in the photo.
Pruning & SizeIt builds its own pyramid — 12–20 ft tall, 8–15 ft wide — and needs almost no pruning. If shaping is wanted, prune lightly in late winter or early spring, before the spring flowers open, so the berry crop is not cut away. Never shear it into a ball; step back and snip stray leaders instead.
Flowers & BerriesSmall, creamy-white, lightly fragrant flowers open in clusters in the leaf axils in spring (March–May). Being perfect flowers, they pollinate themselves — and can pollinate other hollies nearby. The fruit ripens orange-red, about ¼ inch across, in fall and holds through winter as songbird food.

✂️ Propagation — Cuttings Keep the Cultivar

  1. Take semi-hardwood cuttings in summer. Choose current-season shoots whose bases have begun to firm and color, and cut pieces about 4–6 inches long, just below a leaf node.
  2. Strip and trim. Remove the lower leaves, keep two or three at the tip, and clip oversized leaves in half across the blade — less leaf, less water lost while there are no roots.
  3. Dip in rooting hormone. A hormone dip on the cut base is the difference between a cutting that sulks and one that strikes.
  4. Stick them in grit. Set the bases in a sharp, free-draining mix (pine bark and perlite serves well), water in, and hold them humid under cover in bright shade — moist air, never soggy mix.
  5. Wait, then pot on. Roots form over the following weeks. When a gentle tug meets resistance, pot each cutting on and grow it a season before it faces the open ground.
🌿 Why cuttings? A berry’s seed grows a wild holly, not an Oakland — the cultivar’s tight pyramid and perfect flowers live only in its wood. Every Oakland in every nursery is a cutting (or a graft) of that one Mississippi branch, which is also why yours will berry alone: the self-fertile flowers are in its inheritance.

🩺 Troubleshooting

Yellow leaves, green veinsChlorosis — the soil is too sweet. Hollies feed poorly on iron in high-pH ground. Feed with an acid-forming holly fertilizer and mulch with pine bark or leaf litter; new growth greens first.
Browned, scorched leaf edgesLeaf scorch — winter wind or hot afternoon sun on a thirsty plant. Water deeply before hard freezes, mulch the root zone, and give exposed plants a windbreak at their backs.
Sudden leaf dropUsually weather, not death: a sharp cold snap or a dry spell makes hollies shed older inner leaves. Scratch a twig — green under the bark means patience, and spring refills the plant.
Blotched, tunneled leavesHolly leafminer — a tiny fly larva feeding between the leaf’s skins. Pick off and destroy mined leaves; a healthy plant shrugs off a light year of it.
Sticky leaves, black sooty filmScale or whitefly overhead, and sooty mold growing on their honeydew. Wash the film off, treat the insects (horticultural oil serves), and the mold starves.
Few or no berriesThe plant is young, too shaded, or was pruned after the spring flowers opened. Berries follow flowers — shape in late winter, feed in spring, and give it sun and seasons.
⚠️

Berries & leaves — toxic if eaten. Holly fruit and foliage carry compounds that cause stomach upset, vomiting, and diarrhea when eaten. The ASPCA lists hollies (Ilex species) as toxic to cats, dogs, and horses — enjoy the berries on the branch, where they belong to the birds, and keep them out of reach of animals and small children. ASPCA Poison Control: (888) 426-4435.

🌿 Reading Your Photo

Keep it watered through its first dry spells, leave the leaf litter where it falls, and resist the shears — the pyramid is already drawn. In a few springs the cream flowers will come, and because they are perfect, the orange-red berries will follow them on this one plant alone.
